title: Higher Education and AI in Mexico and the United States: Who Is Ready for the Machine?
author: Norma Sancho
summary: Norma Sancho contrasts the United States's anxiety over generative AI in higher education with Mexico's much deeper and older structural problem: a national adult population where, per 2020 census data, only 14.27 percent of Mexicans aged 40 to 84 reached even four years of university education, versus more than one in three comparably aged Americans. Her argument is that AI arrived in a country never equipped to distinguish machine-generated fluency from genuine knowledge, and that Mexico's disadvantage is compounded by the fact that, unlike the United States, it 'did not build the technological order now arriving in its classrooms' — it received AI as an import rather than participating in creating it, per Stanford's 2026 AI Index data on notable model production. Sancho's sharpest argument concerns what AI has actually done to educational assessment everywhere, not just in Mexico: it has made 'the appearance of competence extremely cheap,' producing what she calls 'syntax without thought, bibliography without reading, argument without comprehension' — a problem she considers more serious than plagiarism because it undermines whether any student work can still tell an educator what the student actually knows. Her final and most provocative move is generational: she argues that today's anxious adults, educators, and policymakers are themselves products of the very educational culture whose weaknesses AI is now exposing, since 'millennials and Generation Z inherited an educational culture; they did not invent it' — meaning the crisis long predates ChatGPT.
points: Sancho's headline statistic — only 14.27 percent of Mexicans aged 40-84 reaching four years of university education, versus over one in three comparably aged Americans — reframes 'AI and education' debates in Mexico as secondary to a much older, unresolved structural gap in educational attainment.

Her distinction between countries that built AI and countries that merely 'received the machine,' grounded in Stanford AI Index model-production data, adds a geopolitical dimension often missing from discussions of AI's effect on classrooms and assessment.

The claim that AI has made 'the appearance of competence extremely cheap' — enabling 'syntax without thought, bibliography without reading, argument without comprehension' — identifies a problem more fundamental than plagiarism: that student work may no longer reliably signal what a student actually knows, in any country.
quotes: Higher education in the United States is no longer a source of national pride, but of serious academic concern, largely because of the incursion of so-called 'artificial intelligence.'

In 2020, Mexico had 43,282,914 people between the ages of forty and eighty-four. Of them, only 6,176,550 had reached at least four years of university education or postgraduate study. That is 14.27 percent.
Among Mexicans of exactly the same age, barely one in 6.6 reached our Mexican threshold. The American rate was 2.37 times the Mexican rate.
Mexico is not confronting a technology it created. It is confronting a technology it received.
We can now have syntax without thought, bibliography without reading, argument without comprehension.
This seems to me far more serious than the usual discussion about plagiarism. The larger one is whether the work tells us anything anymore about what the student actually knows.
Millennials and Generation Z inherited an educational culture; they did not invent it.
